content.text:
Yes—but with a caveat: **most “new genres” in the 21st century are really new labels, subgenres, markets, or movements**, not wholly unprecedented forms. Literature usually evolves by recombining older traditions.

Notable examples:

- **Cli-fi / climate fiction** — Fiction centered on climate change and ecological crisis. Climate-related novels existed earlier, but the term *cli-fi* is generally credited to Dan Bloom around **2007–2008**, and it gained wider media attention in the 2010s. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_fiction?utm_source=openai))

- **Solarpunk** — A speculative genre/aesthetic imagining sustainable, community-oriented, often technologically optimistic futures. The term *solarpunk* was coined in a **2008** blog post proposing it as a new literary genre. ([builtin.com](https://builtin.com/articles/solarpunk?utm_source=openai))

- **Hopepunk** — A term for fiction emphasizing resistance, kindness, solidarity, and hope in grim circumstances. It became prominent in the late 2010s; Collins listed it among notable new terms in **2019**. Some critics treat it more as a tone or ethos than a full genre. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopepunk?utm_source=openai))

- **LitRPG** — Fiction that incorporates role-playing-game mechanics—levels, stats, quests, skill trees—into the narrative itself. The term became established in the 2010s, especially through online fiction, self-publishing, and audiobook communities. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LitRPG?utm_source=openai))

- **Romantasy** — A publishing category blending romance and fantasy, especially prominent in the 2020s. Romance-fantasy hybrids are older, but *romantasy* has emerged as a major market label for books where the romantic arc is as central as the fantasy plot. ([infinityideas.studio](https://infinityideas.studio/en/curiosities-of-literature/romantasy-hopepunk-and-cli-fi-are-the-genres-that-will-dominate-the-publishing-market-in-2026/?utm_source=openai))

- **New Weird** — A hybrid of fantasy, horror, science fiction, and surrealism associated especially with writers like China Miéville and Jeff VanderMeer. It has roots in older weird fiction, but as a named contemporary movement it belongs largely to the late 20th/early 21st-century literary landscape. ([ebsco.com](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/literature-and-writing/new-weird-literary-movement?utm_source=openai))

- **Cozy fantasy / cozy speculative fiction** — Gentle, low-stakes fantasy or SF focused on community, healing, food, craft, friendship, or everyday life rather than epic conflict. The ingredients are old, but the label and market identity have grown strongly in the 2020s.

So the short answer is: **yes, several recognizable genres or subgenres have emerged this century**, especially in speculative fiction and online/self-published ecosystems. The bigger shift may be that genres now emerge faster because readers, writers, fandoms, publishers, and algorithms can converge around a label very quickly.
